rationale: Bakker (2003) is a conceptual political-economy synthesis and typology paper ('other' study design, drawing on descriptive global PPI/WHO statistics and secondary urban case examples) analyzing modes of urban water privatization, concessions, corporatization, and public/private/community ownership models in the global South ('regulatory_model_ownership'). Secondary rule mechanisms discussed include full-cost-recovery tariffs, connection charges, and subsidies ('fees_tariffs_subsidies'), land-tenure and cadastral prerequisites in informal settlements ('eligibility_status_documentation'), and municipal bylaws restricting or charging for private well self-provision ('enforcement_sanctions'). On the outcome side, the paper's central 'archipelago vs network' framing focuses on spatial fragmentation of piped network coverage and household connections ('primary_connection'), while co-equally examining institutional/governance transformations ('administrative_outcome'), tariff affordability ('economic_access'), and service intermittency/quality ('effective_access'), warranting 'multiple' for assigned_outcome_label_with_multiple.
